evidence.label: Gigli’s distributional curvature characterization of Alexandrov spaces
Weak Hessian bounds along every geodesic in RCD spaces

headline: Claims Gigli's conjecture: Alexandrov curvature bounds match RCD spaces with a distributional sectional curvature bound.
scope: Complete separable metric spaces in every integer dimension n ≥ 2, with Hausdorff measure as reference measure and Gigli's original global test classes.
plain: There are two ways to say a rough space curves at least as much as a model surface. One compares the shapes of triangles, and the other uses calculus, through a weak version of the curvature tensor defined by Gigli. Gigli conjectured that the two agree on a well-behaved class of rough spaces called RCD spaces. The paper claims this in every dimension of at least two. A Lean proof covers only a supporting result from the companion paper.
doesNot: This does not cover spaces whose reference measure is not exactly Hausdorff measure, or reduced versions of the RCD condition. The main equivalence has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Nicola Gigli, who defined the distributional curvature tensor and posed the conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to connect the triangle and calculus views of sectional curvature on non-smooth spaces, as Gigli conjectured.

explanation:
Start with a triangle on a unit sphere. Take the north pole and two points on the equator a quarter-turn apart. Each side has length π/2, about 1.571, and each angle is 90 degrees. Now draw a flat triangle with the same three side lengths. Its angles are 60 degrees. Measure from one corner to the middle of the opposite side. On the sphere this distance is π/2, about 1.571. In the flat triangle it is (√3/2) × (π/2), about 1.360. The sphere's triangle is fatter. That is what curvature at least 0 means in triangle terms.

In an Alexandrov space with curvature at least κ, small triangles are at least as fat as on a model surface of curvature κ[1]. This needs only distances, not smoothness. The other view uses calculus. An RCD space is a rough space with a lower bound on Ricci curvature, an averaged form of curvature, defined by optimal transport[2]. Optimal transport studies the cheapest way to move mass from one place to another. Gigli defined a distributional sectional curvature on such spaces, tested against smooth-like functions, and conjectured the two views agree[3]. His construction did not by itself link a lower bound on the tensor to triangle comparison[4].

The paper claims the equivalence in every dimension n of at least 2[5]. With Hausdorff measure, the Alexandrov bound κ holds exactly when the space is RCD with distributional sectional curvature at least κ[5]. Hausdorff measure is the natural n-dimensional volume. The choice of that exact measure matters, since it rules out collapsed spaces[6]. The test classes are Gigli's original global ones[7].

The hard direction goes from calculus to triangles. A weak Hessian bound is tested against volume, but a single geodesic, a shortest path, can lie in a set of zero volume[8]. The companion paper bridges this gap. It proves that a weak upper bound on the Hessian, the table of second derivatives, holds along every shortest path[9]. The main paper also needs frames along paths at every time, not only almost every time[10].

How sure is this? The Lean scope note says the formalization carries a weak Hessian upper bound to every shortest path in an RCD space of finite dimension. That is the companion paper's theorem. The main equivalence is not in that note. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if it holds. Lean covers only the companion paper's Hessian-along-geodesics theorem, not the main equivalence. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A metric space where small triangles are at least as fat as matching triangles on a model surface of constant curvature.
A possibly rough space with a lower bound on Ricci curvature, defined by optimal transport, and with a Hilbert-space calculus.
An averaged form of curvature that controls how volume spreads out.
How much a space bends along one flat two-dimensional slice.
Defined by testing against nice functions instead of point by point.
A natural way to measure n-dimensional volume using only distances.
A shortest path between two points.
The table of second derivatives of a function.

claims.text: A complete separable metric space is an n-dimensional Alexandrov space of curvature at least κ if and only if, with Hausdorff measure, it is a full-support RCD((n−1)κ,n) space with distributional sectional curvature at least κ.
claims.sourceLine: a complete separable metric space is an \(n\)-dimensional Alexandrov
claims.sourceQuote: For every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\), we prove that a complete separable metric space is an \(n\)-dimensional Alexandrov space of curvature at least \(\kappa\) if and only if, with reference measure \(\mathcal H^n\), it is a full-support \(\RCD((n-1)\kappa,n)\) space whose distributional sectional curvature is at least \(\kappa\) in Gigli's original global test classes.
